messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hairdresser
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 72

He is 58 years old, an African man who has spent most of his adult life working as a hairdresser, a trade he describes with pride because it has always allowed him to speak with people, make them feel better, and keep his hands busy. Before the robbery, his days have a steady rhythm. He opens his shop early, arranges his clippers and combs, greets familiar clients, and talks easily while he works. He is married and says his wife has long known him as calm, sociable, and careful with money. He has built a life around routine, family, and the small confidence that comes from knowing his neighborhood and his customers.

That changes on an evening when he is leaving work with the day’s earnings. He is walking to his car, tired but satisfied, when two men approach him quickly. At first he thinks they want directions. Then one of them grabs him, and he sees a weapon. In the seconds that follow, everything becomes unreal and sharp at the same time: the demand for money, the pressure in his chest, the fear that he will be killed over what is in his pocket. He gives them what they want, but they keep him on the ground, searching him, shouting, and humiliating him. He remembers the smell of dust and sweat, the sound of his own breathing, and the strange thought that if he stays very still, he might disappear. When they finally run off, he is left trembling, lying in the dark, stunned by the speed with which an ordinary evening has turned into terror.

In the days after the mugging, he does not feel like himself. He says he cannot stop replaying the scene, as if his mind drags him back to the moment the weapon appeared. Certain things—footsteps behind him, men standing too close, a sudden shout—make his body react before he can think. His heart pounds, his muscles tighten, and he feels the same helplessness rise up again. At home, he becomes jumpy and irritable. His wife notices that he checks the locks repeatedly and looks out the window whenever he hears voices outside. He begins to avoid going out after dark and no longer wants to walk the short distance from his shop to his car. He changes the way he works, asking clients to leave before evening if possible, and sometimes he closes early even when the day is going well.

Over time, the robbery reshapes how he experiences the world. He sits in his chair at the salon and scans the street instead of listening fully to his clients. He has trouble concentrating on the simple tasks that once came naturally, such as remembering an appointment or matching a requested haircut exactly. He finds himself startling at the opening of the door or at a car backfiring outside. At night, sleep does not come easily. He lies awake thinking about what might have happened if the men had decided to stab him, or if he had resisted, or if no one had found him afterward. When he does sleep, he wakes suddenly, drenched in sweat, with his chest tight and his mind already searching for danger.

He carries a strong sense of vulnerability that he had not known before. Before the mugging, he had thought of himself as a man who managed his life responsibly. Afterward, he feels exposed in a way that is hard to explain. He no longer trusts crowded streets, and even errands that once seemed ordinary now feel like risks he must calculate carefully. He is embarrassed by how much the event has changed him. He misses his former ease with customers and friends, and he notices that he speaks less, laughs less, and keeps more to himself. His wife encourages him to rest, but he feels restless and on edge, unable to settle into rest without feeling that he is letting his guard down.

As he talks about the robbery, it is clear that the event has become more than a memory; it has altered the way he moves through his days. The shop is still open, the scissors still in his hands, but he works with a vigilance that was not there before, as though safety can disappear in an instant if he is not watching closely enough.
